title: With Due Respect (Vol. 5) -- Ch. 4: Criticisms of the Panganiban Formula
primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5) -- CJP's July 22, 2007 follow-up answering critics of his party-list 'Panganiban Formula,' from Rep. Satur Ocampo's charge of anti-progressive bias to the mathematical objections of Oscar Franklin Tan, Felix Muga II and Luis Baltazar

His rebuttals: that the formula's 'distortions' merely 'reflect the distortions in the law' it converts; that 'rounding off' suits 'abstract math' but not 'flesh-and-blood law' that demands 'at least two percent'; and that the topnotcher's seat-per-2-percent rule flows from the law itself

His structural point that the critics' 'obsession to fill up the 20-percent allocation' (to 53 or 55 seats) would push the House past the constitutional ceiling of 250 members -- meaning 'more salaries, more allowances, and more pork barrel,' all requiring a law

His conclusion that the real fix is for Congress to amend the law (on the allocation, thresholds, limits, rounding and House size), since these are 'policy matters... of Congress,' not the Court -- for 'the Supreme Court does not make the law, it merely applies it'
sub_topics: Ocampo's charge: Rep. Satur Ocampo alleged the formula aimed to 'marginalize, if not eliminate, progressive party-list groups,' which CJP rejects as 'unfair, uncalled for, and totally baseless' -- 'no partisan or ideological bias' entered the Court's deliberations

Tan's objections: Oscar Franklin Tan argued the formula failed to justify the 'two percent per seat ratio' for the first party and to observe proportional representation (no 'rough straight line when graphed'), and proposed filling the 20-percent allocation by discarding the 2-percent threshold (which he called 'mathematically absurd') and seating even 1-percent parties

Muga's and Baltazar's responses: Felix Muga II called Tan's formula 'unacceptable' for itself violating proportional representation and noted perfect proportionality needs the three-seat limit junked too; Luis Baltazar argued both schemes wrongly discarded inviolable parameters and instead proposed 'rounding off' (e.g., above 1.5 percent to 2), reaching 53 seats (his '20 percent' of the House)

Rebuttal one -- distortions reflect the law: any failure to graph a 'rough straight line' arises 'only because the formula reflects the distortions in the law,' since 'the Court merely converted legal provisions into a mathematical formula'

Rebuttal two -- no rounding in 'flesh-and-blood law': rounding 'may make sense in abstract math' but not when 'Sec. 1 (b)... is clear' that only parties 'receiving at least two percent' qualify -- so 199,000 votes cannot satisfy a 200,000-vote 2-percent requirement

Rebuttal three -- the seat-per-2-percent rule: the first party gets 'one seat for every multiple of 2 percent,' derived from the law's mandate that 2 percent earns one seat, with proportionality then applying to the additional seats

Rebuttal four -- the constitutional ceiling: the 'obsession to fill up the 20-percent allocation' (53 or 55 seats, given 212 district representatives) 'may collide with' the Constitution's cap of 'not more than two hundred fifty members, unless otherwise fixed by law' -- making the allocation mandatory would mean 265-267 lawmakers and 'more salaries, more allowances, and more pork barrel,' all of which 'require a law'

The solution: the cure for the 'mathematically obsessed critics' is to 'amend the law' (on the allocation, thresholds, limits, rounding and an automatic House increase), since 'perfect proportionality' is attainable only without thresholds and limits -- but those are 'policy matters addressed to the discretion of Congress,' not the Court; despite seven years and 'active' party lists, Congress has not amended the law, so the Court cannot be faulted for reiterating the formula, confident that 'Congress -- by its inaction -- agrees,' because the provisions, however 'unwise or mathematically imprecise,' are 'not unconstitutional' -- 'the Supreme Court does not make the law, it merely applies it'

stances.claim: The charge that the formula was meant to 'marginalize... progressive party-list groups' is 'unfair, uncalled for, and totally baseless' -- 'no partisan or ideological bias ever crept into the Court's deliberations.'
stances.rhetorical_move: flat rebuttal: meeting an accusation of bias with a categorical denial

stances.claim: The formula's mathematical 'distortions' are not the Court's fault: it 'merely converted legal provisions into a mathematical formula,' and the law's clear 'at least two percent' rule forbids the 'rounding off' that critics want.
stances.rhetorical_move: shift-the-blame-to-the-statute: locating the imperfection in the law, not the math

stances.rhetorical_move: separation-of-powers close: redirecting the fix to the legislature and disclaiming judicial policymaking

notable_anecdotes: Answering the bias charge: CJP firmly rejects Rep. Ocampo's claim that the formula targeted progressives, insisting 'no partisan or ideological bias' shaped the Court's work.
199,000 isn't 2 percent: he illustrates why 'rounding off' fails in law -- if 200,000 votes equal 2 percent, then 199,000 simply does not satisfy 'at least two percent.'
Past 250 means a new law: he warns that filling the 20-percent allocation to 53-55 seats would push the House to 265-267, beyond the constitutional cap, requiring legislation.

Seven years of silence: he notes that despite the Veterans decision flagging the difficulties, Congress had not amended the law in seven years -- so the Court reiterates the formula, reading inaction as agreement.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's July 22, 2007 follow-up column, answers the critics of his party-list 'Panganiban Formula.' He first rejects Rep. Satur Ocampo's charge that the formula was meant to 'marginalize... progressive party-list groups' as 'unfair, uncalled for, and totally baseless,' insisting 'no partisan or ideological bias' shaped the Court's deliberations. He then takes up the mathematical objections: Oscar Franklin Tan faulted the formula for not justifying the 'two percent per seat ratio' and not graphing as a 'rough straight line,' and would discard the 2-percent threshold (which he called 'mathematically absurd') to seat even 1-percent parties; Felix Muga II called Tan's scheme 'unacceptable' and noted true proportionality also needs the three-seat limit junked; and Luis Baltazar proposed 'rounding off' (above 1.5 to 2 percent) to reach 53 seats. CJP rebuts: any failure to graph a straight line arises 'only because the formula reflects the distortions in the law' it converts; 'rounding off may make sense in abstract math' but not in 'flesh-and-blood law' that demands 'at least two percent' (so 199,000 votes cannot satisfy a 200,000-vote requirement); and the topnotcher's seat-per-2-percent rule flows from the statute itself. Crucially, the critics' 'obsession to fill up the 20-percent allocation' (to 53 or 55 seats) would push the House past the constitutional ceiling of 'not more than two hundred fifty members,' meaning 265-267 lawmakers and 'more salaries, more allowances, and more pork barrel' -- all requiring a law. The remedy, he concludes, is for Congress to amend the statute (on the allocation, thresholds, limits, rounding and House size), since these are 'policy matters addressed to the discretion of Congress'; despite seven years of party-list practice Congress has not acted, so the Court cannot be faulted for reiterating a formula whose provisions, however 'unwise or mathematically imprecise,' are 'not unconstitutional' -- for 'the Supreme Court does not make the law, it merely applies it.'
